evidence: Artificial intelligence is helping historians crack open these mysterious texts.

Now Megyesi and her colleagues are leading efforts to harness the power of AI to crack historic ciphers more efficiently, potentially unlocking a wealth of coded information from the past that has previously been uncrackable.

nary_nodes.label: Charles V letter decoded
evidence: It took Cecile Pierrot, a cryptologist at the French National Institute for Computer Science Research (INRIA) in Nancy, France, and her colleagues six months to gradually unravel the key to a 500-year-old letter from Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, that had been written using 120 different cipher symbols across three pages.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event involving the process of converting encrypted or coded messages into intelligible plain text.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org type directly represents this specific type of event. 'Event' is the most appropriate parent.

nary_nodes.label: Mary Queen of Scots letters decoded
evidence: One recent cipher to do this were a collection of coded letters that were found to have been written by Mary Queen of Scots during her long imprisonment in England.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event involving the process of converting encrypted or coded messages into intelligible plain text.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org type directly represents this specific type of event. 'Event' is the most appropriate parent.

nary_nodes.label: Von Wandersleben letter transcribed by AI
evidence: Michelle Waldispühl, a professor of German linguistics at the University of Oslo in Norway and her colleagues, recently used an online AI platform called Transkribus to transcribe a secret letter written by nobleman Sigismund Heusner von Wandersleben to the Swedish Lord High Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna in 1637 at the height of the 30 Years' War
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event involving the process of converting a document from one form (e.g., handwriting, image) into another (e.g., digital text).
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org type directly represents this specific type of event. 'Event' is the most appropriate parent.

nary_nodes.label: AI deciphers Copiale cipher from photos
evidence: They recently showed how the approach could work for simple codes, where every letter is replaced by a single symbol.
They tested the system on a 105-page manuscript they had already decoded, known as the Copiale cipher, which details the rituals, rules and ideals of an 18th-Century German secret society.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event involving the use of artificial intelligence to decipher encrypted or coded messages.
nary_nodes.type_justification: The event 'AI deciphers Copiale cipher from photos' is a specific instance of AI-assisted cipher decipherment, matching the previously minted 'AICipherDecipherment'.

nary_nodes.label: AI chatbot tested on ciphers
evidence: When the researchers tested their AI chatbot with the Borg cipher, Megyesi and her colleagues found it could translate and decode a 500 symbol extract in a little over 29 minutes.
The team also recently tested the system with two other ciphers they had previously decoded which represent different time periods, languages, types of secret codes and levels of complexity.

nary_nodes.label: AI tool developed for Descrypt project
evidence: Megyesi, Waldispühl and their colleagues are developing their own AI tool to turn handwritten historical texts with obscure symbols or scripts into machine-readable documents as part of the multinational Descrypt project.

nary_nodes.label: AI chatbot tool created
evidence: Megyesi's team have used their work to create an AI chatbot-style tool that combines transcription and decryption in a single step.

evidence: Waldispühl and her colleagues in the Descrypt project have been scouring old archives in search of cipher scripts to compile into a database.

nary_nodes.label: Decoding is like detective work
evidence: "It is like detective work where every symbol, pattern, and partial solution may bring us closer to someone's secrets and to a lost historical world," says Beáta Megyesi

nary_nodes.label: 1% of archive material is encrypted
evidence: According to some estimates, around 1% of the material in archives and libraries around the world is fully or partially encrypted.

nary_nodes.label: Decoding is back and forth
evidence: "It was very much back and forth between the machine and the human validator," says Waldispühl.

nary_nodes.label: AI might work independently
evidence: "Maybe at some point AI can do it completely independently."

nary_nodes.label: AI opens possibilities for rare writing systems
evidence: "This opens up exciting possibilities for rare and non-standard writing systems," says Megyesi.

nary_nodes.label: Combine transcription and decipherment
evidence: "The ultimate goal is to combine transcription and decipherment in one single step."

nary_nodes.label: AI helps with scale, speed, pattern discovery
evidence: "AI helps most with scale, speed, pattern discovery and integration of tasks," says Megyesi.

nary_nodes.label: Solving puzzles and creating methods
evidence: "What excites me is not only the possibility of solving one specific historical puzzle, but the prospect of creating methods that can assist researchers across many different cases," says Megyesi.

nary_nodes.label: Borg cipher concealed remedies
evidence: Its cryptic pages apparently concealed secret remedies "for affections of the human body", according to some text scratched inside the cover.

nary_nodes.label: Healing practices attracted suspicion
evidence: Such healing practices were kept under wraps at the time since they could attract suspicion or even accusations of witchcraft.

nary_nodes.label: Charles V feared assassination
evidence: The decrypted letter revealed Charles V – one of the most powerful men of his time – undone by fear of a plot to kill him.
The king was terrified that an Italian mercenary warlord serving the French king, Francis I, was about to assassinate him.

nary_nodes.label: Von Wandersleben warned of threat
evidence: Hidden behind the cipher were Von Wandersleben's warnings about the threat posed by factions of Sweden's protestant allies in the war.

nary_nodes.label: Von Wandersleben made strategic retreats
evidence: He told Oxenstierna that he had been forced to make strategic retreats from the conflict after being told about a conspiracy among his allies, including Lord Franz Heinrich of Saxony.

nary_nodes.label: AI chatbot to reveal coded text
evidence: The idea would be that researchers, or even the public, could give the chatbot a coded, historical text and have it reveal what is written.

nary_nodes.label: Prevent AI hallucination
evidence: This is important to make sure that the AI is not hallucinating or inventing interpretations.

nary_nodes.label: Phaistos Disc remains undeciphered
evidence: The 4,000 year old Phaistos Disc from Crete, for example, remains undeciphered

nary_nodes.label: Linear A remains undeciphered
evidence: as does the early Greek language 'Linear A'.

nary_nodes.label: Finding data for code cracking is challenging
evidence: Finding equivalent amounts of data for code cracking is challenging.

nary_nodes.label: AI tool improves itself
evidence: The AI tool will also be able to improve itself by incorporating corrections from experts that use it.

nary_nodes.label: AI chatbot combines algorithms and LLMs
evidence: The chatbot combines algorithms for decryption trained on pairs of cipher characters and the text they represent with large language models trained on historical texts from different time periods to help provide clues about a code.

nary_nodes.label: Image recognition algorithms incorporated
evidence: Image recognition algorithms, trained on annotated handwriting, are also being incorporated.

nary_nodes.label: Copiale cipher details secret society rituals
evidence: known as the Copiale cipher, which details the rituals, rules and ideals of an 18th-Century German secret society.

nary_nodes.label: Mary Queen of Scots letters revealed plots and relationship
evidence: They revealed her involvement in plots to regain her throne and her tense relationship with her son, James VI of Scotland and future King James I of England.

nary_nodes.label: Borg cipher filled with treatments
evidence: They discovered the text was filled with thousands of bizarre treatments such as drinking several glasses of high-quality red wine or fermenting a nutmeg in some dough to combat dysentery.

nary_nodes.label: Borg cipher coded with symbols and Arabic
evidence: Known as the Borg cipher, the 408-page-long manuscript is mostly incomprehensible – coded using 34 obscure symbols with a few Roman letters and a front page written in Arabic.

nary_nodes.label: Borg cipher pages damaged
evidence: Some of the pages are also damaged due to their age, making the code even more challenging to read.

nary_nodes.label: Earliest ciphers from Ancient Greece and Rome
evidence: Some of the earliest known ciphers date back to Ancient Greece and Rome.

nary_nodes.label: Coded documents conceal various information
evidence: Together, coded historic documents conceal diplomatic intelligence, the rituals of secret societies, medical knowledge, love affairs or everyday details that people wanted to keep secret.

nary_nodes.label: Decoding can rewrite history
evidence: In some cases, decoding these documents has the potential to rewrite what we know about a famous individual or an entire period of history.

nary_nodes.label: Borg cipher uses substitution cipher
evidence: the Borg cipher, for example, uses a straight-forward substitution cipher, meaning that each symbol was swapped with a single Roman letter to hide what was written.

nary_nodes.label: Ciphers can be difficult to unravel
evidence: Others, however, can be difficult to unravel.
In some cases, nothing is known about the original language the uncoded text was written in.
Extra, meaningless symbols can also be inserted as a decoy to throw off anyone hoping to snoop on the text.
In other cases, several signs can be used to represent the same letter.

nary_nodes.label: Decoding requires huge effort
evidence: This can mean a huge amount of work – often involving trial and error – to decode even a small amount of text.

nary_nodes.label: Transcription is painstaking and difficult
evidence: Before code-breaking can begin, researchers must first painstakingly transform a handwritten cipher into a digital document that can be fed into code-cracking software.
Bad handwriting and fading of the ink can make this task even harder.

nary_nodes.label: Pierrot takes a day to transcribe
evidence: Pierrot says it typically takes her a day just to transcribe a two-page letter containing symbols that are unfamiliar to her.

nary_nodes.label: Transkribus trained on various styles
evidence: The tool has been trained on various languages, scripts and handwriting styles that cover several centuries.

nary_nodes.label: Transkribus digitizes documents
evidence: After the image of a document is uploaded to the system, the AI detects blocks of texts and individual lines before scanning the whole text character by character to turn it into a digital form.

nary_nodes.label: Transkribus worked well on Von Wandersleben letter
evidence: Although some manual corrections were needed, the tool worked quite well on Von Wandersleben's letter as it was only partly encrypted using numbers separated by dots that were neatly written with clear spaces between them.
Other parts were not coded and simply written in 17th-Century German script.

nary_nodes.label: Existing AI platforms struggle with unusual characters
evidence: Existing AI transcription platforms often struggle when manuscripts are encrypted with unusual characters, such as invented signs, astrological symbols or numbers that are written in an odd way.

nary_nodes.label: Descrypt project develops adaptable models
evidence: "We are developing more adaptable models trained and tested across a broad range of scripts, alphabets and symbolic repertoires," says Megyesi.

nary_nodes.label: Cryptologists use non-AI software
evidence: At the moment, cryptologists often use specially designed non-AI computer software to help with the task which harnesses algorithms to try to determine what cipher was used and break the code.

nary_nodes.label: Simple ciphers cracked by frequency analysis
evidence: Simple ciphers can often be cracked by analysing the frequency of symbols used and matching them to letters of the alphabet that appear at the same rate in a language.

nary_nodes.label: English letter E is most common
evidence: In English, for example, the letter E is the most common while Z, Q and X are the least frequent.

nary_nodes.label: Von Wandersleben letter used multiple symbols for E
evidence: But in Von Wandersleben's letter from the frontlines of the 30 Years' War, for example, he used up to eight different symbols to represent the letter E.

nary_nodes.label: AI could skip transcription
evidence: Megyesi and her team are now exploring how AI could skip the transcription stage all together, simply by analysing photos of the pages to decipher secret messages.

nary_nodes.label: AI can decipher simple codes from photos
evidence: They recently showed how the approach could work for simple codes, where every letter is replaced by a single symbol.

nary_nodes.label: AI decipherment from photos useful for unknown languages
evidence: Such a system could especially be useful when the underlying language of a cipher is unknown.

nary_nodes.label: Database vital for AI training
evidence: This could prove vital as a way of gathering sufficient data to train an AI capable of cracking codes.

nary_nodes.label: LLMs trained on trillions of words
evidence: Large language models that underpin AI chatbots such as ChatGPT are trained on trillions of words from books, articles and websites.

nary_nodes.label: Postcards are love letters
evidence: The few scraps decoded so far reveal some of these to be love letters written in German.

nary_nodes.label: AI chatbot translated Borg cipher extract in 29 minutes
evidence: Megyesi and her colleagues found it could translate and decode a 500 symbol extract in a little over 29 minutes.
It even provided an English translation.
It also documented the process and explained why the solution was plausible.

nary_nodes.label: AI chatbot quickly decrypted other ciphers
evidence: It quickly decrypted them too, showing that it is capable of tackling a range of ciphers.

nary_nodes.label: AI tools key to cracking elusive ciphers
evidence: Such AI tools could be key to cracking historical ciphers that have been elusive to date.

nary_nodes.label: AI tools help with ancient texts
evidence: They will also help with ancient texts written in alphabets that nobody can read today.

nary_nodes.label: AI skipping transcription research
evidence: Megyesi and her team are now exploring how AI could skip the transcription stage all together, simply by analysing photos of the pages to decipher secret messages.
